newsitem.title: ISRAEL: El Al posted second-quarter profit.
newsitem.headline: El Al posted second-quarter profit.

text.p: State-owned El Al Israel Airlines turned a profit in the second quarter and is expected to end the year with a narrower loss than originally projected, a spokesman for the carrier said on Monday.
"We're finishing the first half in better shape than expected," spokesman Nachman Klieman told reuters.

He declined to provide figures on earnings or revenues for the first six months but said El Al's loss for the full year would be considerably under the $45 million management had forecast. El Al lost about $80 million in 1996.
"As a result of the improvement, we're projecting we'll end up below (a loss of) $40 million," Klieman said.

The airline had a comparatively strong first half, even though foreign tourist arrivals to Israel fell six percent in the period to 1.1 million as security concerns deterred visitors. However,outgoing traffic by Israelis rose eight percent, Klieman said.
"Israelis filled the seats of the missing tourists," he said.
He added that El Al was helped by cost cutbacks, which the airline has been undertaking as it grapples with the second year of declining tourist arrivals.
Klieman said the carrier had replaced Israeli staff overseas with local hires, trimmed back management and had cancelled two unprofitable routes to Sofia and Delhi.

Klieman said Israel was considering shaking up its route structure, in particular increasing Far East routes. He said the airline was weighing introducing twice weekly direct flights to Bangkok in place of a flight that stops in Bombay on the way.

The airline is hoping that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's trip to the Far East scheduled for next week will help win long-sought-after landing rights in Japan. Klieman said Netanyahu would raise the issue with Japanese officials.
Israelis flying to Japan now go to Hong Kong or Bangkok and make connections with other carriers.
Israel's government hopes to privatise El AL next year. A government committee proposed last June that 100 percent of the airline be floated on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
Besides the tourism slump, El Al faces a heavy financial burden from the government's ban on flights during the Jewish Sabbath and holidays.
